title: Distance from the pass mark
prompt: The results email tells each learner how far their final test score was from the pass mark of 70: above it or below it. Write `solve(assessments)` so it returns the score and that distance for every assessment.
rules: Return five columns, in this order: `assessment_id`, `learner_id`, `course_id`, `score` and `margin`.
`score` is `score_pct`, unchanged. `margin` is `score_pct` minus 70: positive above the pass mark, 0 on it, negative below it.
A missing score gives a missing `score` and `margin`. Keep every assessment, duplicates included.
hints: A column minus a number is a new column: `F.col("score_pct") - 70`.
Wrap the arithmetic in brackets before `.alias("margin")`, so the name goes on the whole calculation.
The same column can appear twice in one `select`: once renamed to `score`, once inside the calculation.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(assessments):
    # Return assessment_id, learner_id, course_id, score and margin.
    return assessments
explanation: Both new columns come from `score_pct`: `F.col("score_pct").alias("score")` renames it, and `(F.col("score_pct") - 70).alias("margin")` works out the distance for every row. The brackets matter: `F.col("score_pct").alias("margin") - 70` names only part of the calculation, and the column gets a long generated name instead. A missing score makes the margin missing on its own, because any calculation with a missing value is missing. `70 - score_pct` has the sign the wrong way round: a learner who passed would see a negative number. With SQL text, `selectExpr("assessment_id", "learner_id", "course_id", "score_pct AS score", "score_pct - 70 AS margin")` is the same.
